An orbital in a H-atom is associated with the following radial and angular parts of its wave function
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{$\psi(r) = \dfrac{1}{9\sqrt{30}}\left(\dfrac{Z}{a_0}\right)^{3/2}\sigma^2 e^{-\sigma/2};\quad \psi(\theta,\phi) = \left(\dfrac{15}{4\pi}\right)^{1/2}\sin\theta\cos\theta\cos\phi.$}
Here, $\sigma = \dfrac{2r}{na_0}$, $a_0 = \dfrac{h^2}{4\pi^2 me^2}$, $\theta$ = colatitude, $\phi$ = azimuth.
\bfig{92.5}{SII06_p1_chem_s2_q10_1.png}
Select the correct option(s) regarding this orbital:
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Total energy of electron in it = $-1.51$ eV}
\opt{B}{Orbital angular momentum of electron in this orbital is $\sqrt{6}\,\hbar$}
\opt{C}{ZX plane is not the nodal plane.}
\opt{D}{Orbital can be certainly called $3d_{zx}$ orbital.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\end{bankq}

\opt{B}{The probability of finding the electron in the same-sized volume around x = y = 0, z = a is zero}
\opt{C}{The probability of finding the electron at x = y = z = 0 is zero.}

(i) $\psi_r = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{a_0}\right)^{3/2} e^{-r/na_0}$\par
(ii) $\psi_r = \dfrac{1}{9\sqrt{3}}\left(\dfrac{1}{a_0}\right)^{3/2}(6 - 6\sigma + \sigma^2)e^{-\sigma/2}$\par
(iii) $\psi_r = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\left(\dfrac{1}{a_0}\right)^{3/2}\left(2 - \dfrac{2r}{na_0}\right)e^{-r/na_0}$\par
(iv) $\psi_r = \dfrac{1}{9\sqrt{6}}\left(\dfrac{1}{a_0}\right)^{3/2}(4 - \sigma)\sigma e^{-\sigma/2}$, where $\sigma = \dfrac{2r}{na_0}$\par
Based on above radial functions for different orbitals, select correct statement(s) :
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{for orbital (iv), the graph between $\psi_r$ and r will intersect x axis at two distinct non-zero finite values of r.}
\opt{B}{for orbital (i), the radial probability of finding electron will be maximum at r = a$_0$.}
\opt{C}{for orbital (ii), there is no angular node}
\opt{D}{for orbital (iii), distance of radial node from origin is `2a$_0$'}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

 & List-I & & List-II \\

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SRGBT02-P1-CHEM-S1-G31-32, source={SRGBT - Test 02 (01 Aug 2021)}, questions={31-32}]
Both de--Broglie hypothesis and Heisenberg uncertainty principle establish that microscope particles have more prominent wave nature.\par
Heisenberg realised that, in the world of very small particles one cannot measure any property of a particle without interacting with it in some way. This introduces an unavoidable uncertainty into the result. One can never measure all the properties exactly.\par
Minimum uncertainty in position of any body is given by wavelength of light.\par
\textbf{Heisenberg's uncertainty principle :}\par
$\Delta\mathrm x\;.\;\Delta\mathrm P\;\geq\;\dfrac{\mathrm h}{4\pi}=\dfrac{\hbar}2$\par
(uncertainty in position, uncertainty in momentum)\par
\textbf{De--Broglie hypothesis :}\par
$\lambda=\dfrac{\mathrm h}{\mathrm P}$\par
where $\lambda$ is de--Broglie wavelength of any body having non relativistic momentum P.
\end{bankpassage}
